column3: Near-verbatim parallel: one community under one Lord, with worship specifying the shared response that 23:52 frames as taqwa.
The immediate command to messengers joins lawful provision with righteous work, supplying the practical norm before the unity declaration.
It presents humanity as once one community and then divided, making later disagreement a direct problem for the unity claim.
Its distinction between God's ability to make one community and the persistence of difference qualifies unity as more than enforced uniformity.
The immediate sequel depicts people fragmenting their affair into sects, the clearest local negation of 23:52's one community.
The Lord's protection from punishment does not clarify communal unity or its required response.
The statement that every community received a warner extends the focus's communal horizon across peoples.
The command to leave the fragmented groups in their heedlessness shows the consequence of rejecting the preceding unity.
Naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron confirms a common Lord but adds little to the focus's communal claim.
Inherited allegiance to an ancestral community supplies a concrete rival basis for belonging and guidance.
The nearby question about wealth and children begins the corrective context but does not itself explain unity.
Each community is summoned to its record, preserving communal identity while making its deeds accountable.
Mutual disavowal of deeds does not materially develop the one-community declaration.
Reverent fear of the Lord gives an immediate exemplar of the taqwa required at 23:52.
The promise to empower the oppressed does not explain unity under one Lord.
It directly joins fear of the Lord with faithful conduct, though without a communal-unity dimension.
Faith in the Lord's signs continues the local portrait of the community that answers 23:52 rightly.
The Lord of heavens, earth, and worlds supplies the universal scope of the single Lord named in the focus.
Shared origin and divine lordship are relevant background but do not address a unified community.
The immediate rejection of associating partners with the Lord identifies exclusive lordship as essential to the focus's unity.
Fear of the Lord is tied to a day when familial ties cannot substitute, sharpening the seriousness of taqwa.
The revealed warning that none is god but God concludes with taqwa, closely aligning exclusive deity and the focus's command.
The community's anxious giving because of return to its Lord makes taqwa an active, accountable disposition.
It commands full taqwa and steadfast submission, offering a direct ethical formulation though not the communal premise.
The Lord of heavens and earth grounds the exclusive, universal lordship that holds the focus's community together.
The local diagnosis of hearts in heedlessness shows an obstacle to receiving the unity declaration but adds little detail.
Fear of the Fire gives taqwa an eschatological warning but not its relation to communal unity.
Its warning from God ends with a direct taqwa command, reinforcing the protective response required by the focus.
The nearby assurance of proportionate obligation and truthful record calibrates the communal ethic that follows the focus.
The broad call to taqwa offers only a general parallel to the focus's final command.
The command to fear God within covenantal fidelity is relevant but does not add to shared community or lordship.
The continuation about apparent benefits being misread is local context rather than a clarification of unity.
It applies taqwa to ethical consultation within a believing group, a limited social expression of the focus's command.
The description of those who practice taqwa supplies a general positive outcome without developing communal unity.
Racing toward good deeds completes the nearby portrait of the faithful, but repeats the ethical direction already established.
Cooperation in righteousness and taqwa gives a social form to the command, though its ritual-legal setting is distinct.
The contrast between worldly life and the lasting abode does not clarify the focus's community or lordship.
Earlier communities under hardship do not materially develop one community under one Lord.
The commissioning of Moses to hear revelation does not add to the focus's claim.
Like 11:118, it distinguishes potential forced unity from differentiated outcomes, qualifying what one community can mean.
The transience of worldly life does not clarify communal unity.
Its collective commands culminate in taqwa, giving a general communal discipline but little new explanation.
Moses's admission of past error is unrelated to the focus's unity and taqwa.
Truthful reception is linked to the people of taqwa, but offers only a broad trait already represented.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the one-community declaration.
It identifies God as Lord of a celestial object, supporting exclusive lordship without communal content.
It closely combines shared Lordship, worship, and a straight path, making explicit the common orientation underlying unity.
It again rejects reading one community as imposed sameness and adds individual accountability for deeds.
Pharaoh's claim to supreme lordship forms a sharp contrary claim to the focus's declaration of the true shared Lord.
Its reference to people becoming one community concerns a worldly social condition, not the focus's normative unity.
It repeats the shared-Lord-and-worship formulation, but adds little after the closer parallel at 19:36.
Human ingratitude toward its Lord negatively frames failure to respond to lordship, without communal unity.
God's gathering of all people is a broad collective dimension but does not develop the focus's present community.
Believers seek forgiveness and protection from their Lord, a personal taqwa posture with limited communal relevance.
It directly addresses diverse communities, paths, testing, and competition in good while locating ultimate resolution in God.
Guiding leaders emerge through patience and certainty, offering only an indirect account of communal guidance.
Prayer and taqwa are directed to the one to whom all are gathered, linking the command to a shared ultimate return.
The Lord's full awareness of people supports accountability but does not clarify community unity.
It states that God is our Lord and your Lord while acknowledging distinct deeds, a useful unity-with-accountability parallel.
The lack of protection from God supplies a negative consequence of failed taqwa but adds no communal dimension.
The concise assertion of one deity provides the theological basis for one community under one Lord.
The repeated call to fear God and obey the messenger is a generic instance of the focus's ethical response.
Common human origin and shared taqwa make social relations part of responsibility to one Lord.
Worship of the creator is explicitly ordered toward taqwa, providing a foundational form of the focus's response.
A single blast is not a meaningful parallel to one community.
It repeats the generic fear-and-obedience summons already represented at 26:131.
Different communities have rites, yet one God and submission to Him, directly holding diversity together under one deity.
Guidance for the people of taqwa is relevant but gives no account of communal unity.
It condemns rejecting God when He alone is invoked while accepting association, directly opposing exclusive lordship.
The generic fear-and-obedience summons adds little beyond earlier repetitions.
One God, righteous action, and refusal of association provide a compact individual expression of the focus's unified allegiance.
The complaint about one food and its consequences does not clarify one community under one Lord.
Illicit distinctions over livestock do not explain the focus's communal unity.
The question whether Pharaoh's people will practice taqwa gives only a minimal parallel.
The sleepers' awakening and food mission do not clarify the focus's claim.
Lot's call to taqwa is another generic prophetic summons with little marginal value.
One group persists in warning another so that they may practice taqwa, a limited intra-community application.
The Lord's calculated gift does not clarify unity or the command to fear Him.
It repeats the ancestral-community attachment of 43:22 with little added value.
The prayer for good and protection from punishment is a broad personal expression of taqwa.
The discussion of death and attribution of good or evil does not materially develop the focus.
The immediate later verse exposes the inconsistency of admitting God's ownership while failing to practice taqwa.
It traces a one-community beginning, subsequent dispute, prophetic guidance, and divine adjudication, extending 10:19's pattern.
The Mother of the Book does not clarify the focus's community or command to fear God.
Aversion when the Lord is mentioned alone is a negative response to exclusive lordship, but the setting is indirect.
Collective creation and resurrection as one soul do not explain communal unity under one Lord.
The presence of guardians does not clarify the focus's unity or taqwa.
Taqwa is linked to the life-preserving limit of retaliation, a distinct legal application with limited overlap.
Return to the Lord affirms ultimate dependence but does not develop a unified community.
Flight from close family does not clarify the focus's communal declaration.
The question of human creation does not materially explain one community or taqwa.
The most God-fearing person's rescue supplies an individual outcome of taqwa without communal content.
All being brought before God gives a collective horizon but not the focus's community or response.
The mention of the Lord's mercy to Zachariah does not clarify the focus.
Magnifying the Lord supports recognition of His supremacy but adds little to communal unity.
Universal questioning before the Lord supplies accountability but not the focus's present communal relation.
The sign of restoration after death does not clarify unity under one Lord.
The same taqwa charge is given across successive scriptural communities, extending the focus's obligation beyond one group.
The attempted expulsion of the messenger does not clarify the focus's unity or taqwa.
Warning the central community and its surroundings gives a broad communal scope, but not the focus's unity claim.
The call to a common word centers worship on God alone and rejects taking lords besides Him, directly articulating shared allegiance.
Holding together to God's rope and not dividing gives the focus's one community an explicit communal practice and counter-image.
It directly prohibits becoming divided after clear proofs, sharply clarifying the fragmentation negated by 23:52.
It warns against excess and following communities that went astray, showing how communal deviation can displace right guidance.
The one straight path and the prohibition on divergent paths provide a concrete moral form for unified orientation.
Those who split their religion and become sects supply an explicit opposite to the focus's one community.
A community that guides by truth and acts justly supplies a positive collective expression of unified obedience.
Believing men and women form mutual allies who enjoin right, restrain wrong, and obey God and His messenger.
Every community has a messenger, extending the focus's communal relation to divine guidance across peoples.
The community given a secure dwelling later differed only after knowledge came, reinforcing the distinction between shared provision and division.
It joins worship of God alone with the upright religion, making exclusive authority the basis of a rightly ordered common way.
The proclamation that God is one and that people should take heed directly joins monotheism to the focus's taqwa response.
Sending a messenger to every community with the command to worship God and avoid false powers broadens the focus's pattern historically.
The declaration that God is one God, followed by a command to fear Him alone, is a close theological and ethical parallel.
God's unmatched sovereignty and freedom from partners directly support the focus's single, unshared lordship.
The factions' disagreement after the shared message presents a narrative counterpart to the fracture opposed by 23:52.
The uniform message to every messenger to worship God alone supplies the prophetic basis for one community under one Lord.
Its statement that people split their affair among themselves is the near verbal and thematic counterpart to 23:53's fragmentation.
Each community has its rite while all are directed to their Lord, relating differentiated practice to a common divine authority.
The succession of messengers and the making of rejecting peoples into tales provides the immediate historical setting for the focus's declaration.
Turning to God, practicing taqwa, and establishing prayer gives a collective pattern of return to the one Lord.
Those who divide their religion into sects and delight in their own faction explicitly portray the opposite of one community.
The command to worship God with sincere religion states the undivided devotion assumed by the focus.
Aversion when God alone is mentioned exposes the resistance to exclusive lordship that the focus requires.
One God, uprightness toward Him, and seeking forgiveness form a concise parallel to shared lordship and common orientation.
It commands establishment of religion and forbids division within it, directly explaining unity without erasing distinct communities.
The shared-Lord-and-worship declaration repeats the close formulation found at 19:36 and 3:51.
Sincere worship of God, upright religion, prayer, and almsgiving provide a disciplined communal expression of exclusive devotion.
